shows.title: Modernisms
shows.description:
Adriana Varejão has spent more than thirty years mining the visual legacy of the azulejo, the glazed tile that Portugal exported to its colonies and that Brazil went on to remake as its own. This new body of paintings, timed to coincide with her representation of Brazil at the current Biennale Arte, moves the inquiry out of the Baroque churches and colonial facades that occupied her earlier tile paintings and into the twentieth century, when patterned tilework became a signature surface of Brazilian modernist architecture — cladding apartment blocks, housing estates and public buildings from the 1940s onward.

The paintings translate that architectural skin into oil and plaster on canvas, built up so the surface reads as cracked, glazed ceramic even though it is entirely painted illusion — a technique Varejão has long used to fuse the language of painting with that of tile, wound and wall. Where her Biennale pavilion work leans on religious and Baroque sources, the canvases here draw on an archive the artist has assembled from years of research in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Salvador and Belo Horizonte, focused on the mass-produced geometric and biomorphic patterns that flooded Brazilian facades from the 1970s on.

It's a show about a specific, under-written strand of design history as much as it is a painting exhibition: Varejão treats these industrial patterns as a visual inheritance worth recovering, arguing that Brazilian modernism didn't reject its colonial tile tradition so much as absorb and repurpose it. Seeing this work in Venice, a city built from patterned surfaces of its own, adds an extra layer of resonance, and the show offers a useful counterpoint to her pavilion presentation across town.

shows.title: Chromatic Conditions
shows.description:
Chromatic Conditions is a solo outing of new paintings by Whitney Hagen, built around vivid color fields and shifting geometric planes that suggest architecture without ever quite settling into it. Hagen's abstractions read as studies in perception — hidden structures of space and time rendered through saturated color and layered, tilting forms.

The show takes its cue from the 61st Venice Biennale's theme, In Minor Keys, and Hagen's paintings share that exhibition's interest in subtler registers: quieter color relationships and oblique architectural logic rather than grand gesture. It's a compact, chromatically confident body of work, and a good excuse to see how a younger painter is responding to the Biennale's own curatorial mood.
